title: Gifts for the Dead: How the Games Began
description: Funeral munera, the first fight in Rome in 264 BCE, and how grief turned into politics

concepts.title: Three Pairs in a Cattle Market
concepts.contentHtml:
Forget the Colosseum for a moment. Rome's first recorded gladiator show had no arena at all. In 264 BCE two brothers, Marcus and Decimus Brutus, honoured their dead father in the Forum Boarium, the city's cattle market, by matching three pairs of gladiators.1 Six armed men in a marketplace: that is where nearly seven centuries of Roman blood sport began.

The Romans called such a show a munus (plural munera), a duty or gift. Traditionally a munus was an offering owed to an aristocratic man when he died, rooted in the belief that the spirits of the dead had to be appeased with blood. Later writers, among them the Christian Tertullian, traced the custom to an older practice of killing slaves and captives at the funeral pyre.

Where did the idea come from? Roman tradition credited the Etruscans, their neighbours to the north. The physical evidence points south as well: tomb paintings of the fourth century BCE at Paestum, a Lucanian city in southern Italy, show fighters receiving terrible, plainly fatal wounds.2 The custom may have reached Rome by way of Campania, and early Romans even used "Samnite", the name of a Campanian people Rome had fought, as another word for gladiator.

The religious roots never quite vanished. Even in the imperial arena, an attendant dressed as Charun, the Etruscan escort of the dead, or as Hermes, the god who led souls to the underworld, finished off a fallen fighter with a blow to the forehead. The funeral link survived in private life too: gladiators later fought at the funerals of most people of consequence, even women, and some Romans left money in their wills to pay for a show at their own funeral.

concepts.title: From Grief to Ambition
concepts.contentHtml:
During the Republic the grieving family paid for a munus, and the bigger the show, the grander the family looked. Gradually the ritual lost much of its religious meaning and became openly political, a way for ambitious men to win the crowd. Magistrates staging public festivals sometimes put on immense numbers of fighters precisely to please the people.

No one exploited this better than Julius Caesar. Elected aedile in 65 BCE, he honoured his father, who had died twenty years before, with 320 pairs of gladiators in silvered armour.1 The funeral had become an excuse rather than a reason. A nervous Senate, still mindful of the rebellion of Spartacus, limited the number of gladiators allowed in Rome. In 46 BCE Caesar staged games at the tomb of his daughter Julia, eight years after her death, with plays and beast fights that included the first giraffe seen in Rome. The show was criticised for its extravagance, and his own soldiers protested that none of the money was coming to them.

The emperors finished the job. Augustus handed the games to the praetors and limited them to two shows a year of sixty pairs each, which stopped rivals buying popularity on Caesar's scale. Later emperors took the munera for themselves: after Domitian, only the emperor could present them in Rome, and anyone who wanted to stage games elsewhere needed official permission.

By the end of the second century CE the Christian writer Tertullian could complain that this kind of entertainment "has passed from being a compliment to the dead to being a compliment to the living". In a little over four centuries, a family's debt to its dead had become a state's tool for managing its people.

concepts.title: Bread, Circuses and a Day at the Games
concepts.contentHtml:
The satirist Juvenal gave us the phrase "bread and circuses" (panem et circenses) for the food and shows that kept Rome's crowds content. Under the Antonine emperors about a million people lived in the city, and the arena was one of the few places where they could see their ruler in person and, safe in a crowd of thousands, let him know what they wanted. The emperor was expected to attend, and how he behaved was watched as closely as the fighting.

Here is a surprise: gladiator shows were rare. In Rome they ran perhaps ten or twelve days a year, often around the Saturnalia festival.1 That is far less often than theatre or chariot racing, because gladiator shows were almost never part of the festivals that honoured the gods. A typical munus in Rome featured no more than about 120 pairs. Shows were advertised in red letters by professional sign painters, programmes listed who would fight, and spectators bet on the results.

A full day had a rhythm: wild-beast hunts in the morning, executions of condemned criminals around midday, gladiators in the afternoon. The fighters paraded in, their weapons were shown to be sharp, lots were drawn and a war trumpet sounded. The whole programme acted out Roman order. Wild nature, criminals and foreign enemies were defeated in public, and the gladiator showed the audience how to face death with courage.

Yet the men who embodied those virtues were outcasts. Gladiators were infames, legally disgraced and ranked with criminals and other shameful trades. Tertullian caught the paradox: "They love whom they lower; they despise whom they approve." The fascination ran stranger still. Gladiators' blood was believed to cure impotence, and a bride whose hair was parted with the spear of a defeated gladiator was thought to be in for a fertile marriage.

title: The Colosseum: A Machine for Spectacle
description: Building the Flavian Amphitheatre, its 100-day opening, the hypogeum, the awning and seating by rank

concepts.title: Built on Nero's Lake
concepts.contentHtml:
The Colosseum was a political statement in stone. After the turmoil of civil war, the new Flavian dynasty needed to show that Rome had recovered, and Vespasian's coins proclaimed Roma resurgens, Rome rising again. Vespasian began the building in the early 70s CE on the site of the lake and gardens of Nero's Golden House.1 The lake was drained and concrete foundations six metres deep were laid. The private pleasure grounds of a hated emperor became a public arena.

Its official name was the Flavian Amphitheatre. "Colosseum" probably comes not from the building's size but from a colossal gilded bronze statue of Nero, remade to resemble the sun god, which stood outside until the fourth century. Titus opened the amphitheatre in 80 CE, and his brother Domitian completed it.

The numbers are still startling: four storeys about 45 metres high, an oval 189 by 156 metres, and an arena of about 87.5 by 54.8 metres. Each of the first three storeys had eighty arches, and seventy-six of the entrances were numbered so that spectators could find their seats. Fighters paraded in through the Porta Triumphalis. The dead were carried out through the Porta Libitinensis, named after the goddess of funerals, while losers who had been spared left by the Porta Sanavivaria. The usual estimate is about 50,000 spectators, roughly 45,000 seated and 5,000 standing, though you will also meet figures as high as the 80,000 quoted in Ancient World.

Wait, really? The ruin later had a second life as a garden. In 1844 Richard Deakin catalogued more than 420 plant varieties growing in it, some rare and even unique to the spot, perhaps descended from food brought for the exotic animals centuries before.

concepts.title: A Hundred Days to Open
concepts.contentHtml:
Titus opened the amphitheatre in 80 CE with games that lasted a hundred days.1 The historian Cassius Dio, a senator who lived about a century later, lists the highlights: a battle between cranes, another between four elephants, and animals tame and wild "slain to the number of nine thousand".2 Women, he adds, "not those of any prominence", took part in killing them. Suetonius gives a different number, five thousand wild beasts of every kind in a single day. Ancient totals like these cannot be checked and the sources disagree, but every version is enormous.

Then came water. According to Dio, Titus suddenly filled the same theatre with water and brought in horses and bulls trained to behave in the water as on land, followed by people on ships re-enacting a sea battle between Corcyreans and Corinthians. A larger naval battle, with three thousand men playing "Athenians" and "Syracusans", was fought on an artificial lake outside the city that Augustus had dug for the purpose. Could the Colosseum really be flooded? Probably, but only in its early years: the maze of corridors, cages and lifts that now fills the space under the arena was added by Domitian.

Generosity was part of the show. Titus had little wooden balls thrown down into the crowd, each inscribed with a prize: food, clothing, a silver or gold vessel, horses, pack animals, cattle or even slaves. Whoever caught a ball could claim what it named. The games were the emperor's gift, and everyone was meant to know it.

concepts.title: Lifts, Sails and Seats by Rank
concepts.contentHtml:
The word arena comes from harena, sand, which covered the wooden floor and soaked up the blood. Beneath the floor lay the hypogeum, a basement of service corridors, animal cages, ramps and mechanical lifts. In the late 1990s Heinz-Jürgen Beste of the German Archaeological Institute in Rome noticed patterns of holes, notches and grooves in its walls and worked out that they had held capstans and lifts. By one count there were between 24 and 28 lifts, each able to raise about 600 pounds, roughly two lions.1 Up to eight men turned each capstan, so running every lift at once took more than 200 people. In 2015 a documentary team built a working replica 23 feet tall and used it to lift a wolf into the arena, the first wild animal raised into the Colosseum in over 1,500 years.

Above the crowd hung the velarium, an awning of long fabric strips hung from ropes on 240 masts around the top of the building. A detachment of marines stationed nearby raised and lowered it like a ship's sails. Shade could be a weapon: Suetonius says Caligula sometimes had an awning drawn back when the sun was hottest and gave orders that no one be allowed to leave.

Where you sat showed who you were. The podium nearest the sand was reserved for senators and magistrates, the equestrian order sat behind them, and the tiers rose through the social ranks to wooden seats at the very top. Augustus had ruled that women could watch gladiators only from the upper seats, although men and women had once sat together; only the Vestal Virgins had a place of their own, opposite the praetor's tribunal.

title: Who Fought, and How
description: Captives, convicts and volunteers, life in the gladiator school, and the matched pairs of fighters

concepts.title: Captives, Convicts and Volunteers
concepts.contentHtml:
Most gladiators did not choose the arena. They were prisoners of war, slaves bought for the purpose, or criminals sentenced to the schools. Roman law drew a grim line between two sentences. A man condemned ad gladium, to the sword, had to be killed within a year, while one condemned ad ludum, to a gladiator school, might win his discharge after three years.

Then there were the volunteers, the auctorati. By the end of the Republic, by one modern estimate, free men made up half of those who fought.1 Many were outcasts: freed slaves, discharged soldiers, or retired gladiators coming back for another spell. They signed on for a fee and swore a terrible oath, preserved by the novelist Petronius, to submit to being burned, bound, beaten and killed with the sword. A few aristocrats joined them, to the horror of moralists. Tacitus wrote that the games of 63 CE exceeded all precedent in the number of distinguished women and senators who disgraced themselves in the arena.

Why sign? Money and fame, and for some, nothing left to lose. A gladiator could be adored, yet the law treated him as disgraced. A free man who fought became free again on his discharge, but he could never rise to equestrian rank however rich he later became. Even an emperor felt the pull. Commodus fought as a secutor, boasted of victory in a thousand matches and kept rooms at one of the schools; his entourage had him killed the day before he planned to march from there, dressed as a gladiator, to take up the consulship.

concepts.title: Inside the Ludus
concepts.contentHtml:
The Latin word ludus means both "game" and "school", since both depend on imitation and repetition. A gladiator school was run by a lanista, a manager who trained a troupe (familia) and sold or hired its members to anyone staging a show. Capua, in Campania, was the most famous training centre, and Spartacus broke out of a school there in 73 BCE. After his revolt the state took tighter control, and large numbers of gladiators were trained in imperial schools.

In Rome, Domitian built four schools near the Colosseum, one of them for the beast fighters. The largest, the Ludus Magnus, was linked to the amphitheatre by an underground passage, and each school had its own small oval arena with seats, so the public could watch the fighters train. Recruits practised with wooden swords. Life inside resembled prison, with small cells and shackles, but the food was better and the medical care the best available, because a trained gladiator was an expensive investment. The physician Galen, whom you may have met in History of Medicine, was one of the doctors who treated them.

Radar now lets archaeologists see inside a school. Researchers from the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute for Archaeological Prospection and Virtual Archaeology used ground-penetrating radar to map a ludus at Carnuntum, a Roman city in what is now Austria, one of the top discoveries of 2011. The fourth-century school, the fourth largest ever found, is a self-enclosed complex with an inner courtyard, a circular training area, living quarters and a cemetery, plus under-floor heating and a bathing area.1 A gladiator who survived long enough could retire with a wooden sword, the rudis, as a token of discharge, and such veterans were called rudiarii.

concepts.title: Matched Pairs: Net Against Sword
concepts.contentHtml:
Gladiators came in types, each with its own kit and style, and the art lay in the pairing. Fighters were meant to be evenly matched but not identically armed, so the advantage of one was offset by the strength of the other.1 Similar types rarely fought each other. Fans split into supporters of the small-shield men and the big-shield men, and emperors had favourites: Caligula and Titus backed the Thracians, Domitian the murmillones.

  • Retiarius ("net man"): a net, a three-pronged trident and a dagger, no helmet, and only a guard on the left shoulder. He was the most lightly armed of all.
  • Secutor ("chaser"), his usual opponent: a distinctive helmet, a large curved shield, a short sword, a padded sleeve on the sword arm and a greave on the leading left leg. Isidore of Seville said the pair stood for water against fire, Neptune against Vulcan.
  • Murmillo, named for the fish on his helmet crest, armed with a short sword and big shield, often matched against the thraex ("Thracian"), who carried a curved short sword and a small square shield.

Tactics followed from kit. The secutor had to close in fast behind his shield, because heavy armour and a helmet that restricted his breathing would soon exhaust him. The retiarius kept his distance, swinging his net and thrusting at head and legs, hoping to entangle his man and finish him with the dagger.

Every bout had a referee, the summa rudis, named after the rod he carried, who could enforce the rules and stop a fight. A beaten fighter laid down his shield and raised a finger, usually of the left hand, to ask for mercy. If neither man prevailed, both could be released standing, stantes missi: the Roman draw.

title: How Often Did Gladiators Die?
description: Death rates over time, why losers were spared, how the evidence is read, and the Ephesus cemetery

concepts.title: Fight to the Death? Usually Not
concepts.contentHtml:
Films end every bout with a corpse. The evidence says otherwise, at least for much of Rome's history. Alfonso Manas of the University of California, Berkeley, has studied the results of fights painted on the walls of Pompeii. In the first century CE, he finds, about one fight in five ended with the death of the loser, and the rate probably stayed similar in the second century.1 Another estimate puts a professional's chance of being killed in any one bout at that time at perhaps one in ten. The two figures agree better than they look. Each fight has two fighters, so if one fight in five kills somebody, each man's risk per bout is about one in ten.

The rate moved over time. Fourth-century BCE tomb paintings at Paestum show horrific wounds, so early fights were often lethal. Reforms after 27 BCE, under Augustus and Tiberius, seem to have cut deaths, and as the danger fell some free men volunteered. In the third century CE the rate rose again: fights in which the loser was not allowed to ask for pardon became customary, and Manas reads the sources of that century as showing one fight in two ending in death.

Why spare a loser? Partly money. Magistrates rented gladiators from their owners, and according to Virginia Campbell of the Open University, surviving contracts suggest that a gladiator returned badly injured or dead turned the lease into a sale, at a price perhaps fifty times the original fee.2 A crowd-pleasing pardon could also save a host a fortune.

None of this applied to everyone in the arena. Criminals condemned to die, sent to the beasts or to the midday executions, had no hope of survival. The philosopher Seneca, who once wandered in at lunchtime, was appalled: "The outcome of every fight is death."

concepts.title: Reading the Scoreboard
concepts.contentHtml:
How can anyone count deaths from two thousand years away? Historians lean on a few kinds of evidence, and each has its own bias.

  • Painted results and graffiti. At Pompeii, fight results were painted on walls, and these are what the one-in-five figure rests on. Fighters and fans also scrawled boasts, such as "Celadus the Thracian, thrice victor and thrice crowned, the young girls' heart-throb."
  • Mosaics. Fourth-century mosaics from Torrenova show the losers of a whole series of fights lying dead, which supports the idea that the late empire was bloodier.
  • Medallions and monuments. A medallion from Cavillargues, now in the archaeological museum at Nîmes, dates to the late second or early third century CE and shows a retiarius and a secutor named Xantus and Eros, with fifteen and sixteen victories, under the words STANTES MISSI, "released standing". Both men walked out alive.
  • Tombstones and graves. Gladiators appear on funerary monuments across the empire, and at Ephesus (next concept) the graves carried tombstones carved with different gladiator types.

Each source tilts the picture. Painted results survive only where walls do, mostly at Pompeii. Monuments were paid for by survivors, owners or fans, so they favour stars and winners, while the many who died young and unknown left nothing. Even so, the sources point the same way: in the first two centuries CE death was a real risk in every bout, but most fights ended with the loser alive.

How long did gladiators live? Most of the men buried at Ephesus died as young adults between 20 and 30. That sounds brutal, and it was, but set it against Roman life in general: by one estimate, three in every five Romans did not survive to their twentieth birthday.

concepts.title: The Gladiator Cemetery at Ephesus
concepts.contentHtml:
For centuries gladiators were known almost only from texts and pictures; their bones were missing. Then, in 1993, a gladiator cemetery was discovered at Ephesus, the great Roman city near the Aegean coast of Turkey.1 It dates to the second and third centuries CE and lay at the northern foot of Panayırdağ hill, about 300 metres east of the ancient stadium. The graves had plain walls and fixed tombstones showing different types of gladiators.

Excavating it was hard. The bones lay in a layer about three metres thick within an area of only 20 square metres, mixed together because the site had been used again and again over a long period, so the team recovered them with methods developed for mass graves. A minimum of 68 individuals were excavated, nearly all of them men.

The skulls tell the story. Eleven showed well-healed injuries from earlier fights, and ten had injuries received around the time of death, made by both blunt and sharp force and consistent with arena combat.2 One wound has been read as the mark of a trident. The healed fractures matter as much as the fatal ones: they show injured gladiators surviving, being treated and fighting again. Researchers from Vienna, among them Fabian Kanz and Karl Grossschmidt, argue that the trauma pattern confirms what written sources say about the rules of gladiator fights.

There was a surprise. Among the dead lay a single woman, the only female found in the cemetery, and her isotope values suggest she may have come from another region. Nothing in the grave tells us who she was.

title: Bodies of Evidence: Diet, Bones and a Lion's Bite
description: The barley men, the plant-ash drink from the Ephesus bones, and York's headless men and the lion's bite

concepts.title: The Barley Men
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture a gladiator and you probably picture a slab of muscle fed on steak. The Romans saw something different. Pliny the Elder called gladiators hordearii, "barley eaters", and it was not a compliment.1 The physician Galen wrote that beans were an important part of their diet while they ate little meat, and their training diet had its own name, gladiatoria sagina.

In 2014 a team led by Sandra Lösch and Fabian Kanz tested this against the bones. They measured stable isotopes in bone collagen from 53 people buried at Ephesus, 22 of them gladiators. The method works because food leaves chemical fingerprints. Carbon isotopes separate C3 plants such as wheat and barley from C4 plants such as millet, and nitrogen isotopes rise the higher up the food chain you eat, so a heavy meat eater shows high nitrogen values.

The results matched the ancient texts, with a twist. Everyone, gladiator or not, lived mainly on C3 plants like wheat and barley, and the gladiators' carbon, nitrogen and sulphur values did not differ significantly from those of ordinary townspeople.2 Nitrogen values at Ephesus were low compared with other Roman sites, which suggests plenty of legumes. So if you have heard that gladiators were vegetarians, that goes too far. The isotopes show a grain-and-bean diet much like everyone else's, and the two highest nitrogen values in the sample belonged to gladiators, a sign of regular animal protein.

The gladiators were also a mixed group. Their values spread across more than one step of the food chain, and two of them had carbon and sulphur signatures that point to childhoods in other regions. That fits what the texts say about recruitment: gladiators were gathered from all over the empire.

concepts.title: A Drink of Ash
concepts.contentHtml:
The strangest result from Ephesus came from a second test. The team measured the ratio of strontium to calcium (Sr/Ca) in the bone mineral. Strontium has no known function in the body, but it travels with calcium through the food chain and settles in bones and teeth in its place, so the ratio reflects where your calcium came from. The gladiators' ratios were significantly higher than those of the other inhabitants of Ephesus, and their mean strontium content was about 460 micrograms per gram of bone against about 245.

What could explain it? The authors point to a drink described by Pliny the Elder in his Natural History: a beverage made of stove ashes that played a role in gladiators' lives, taken after fights and perhaps after training to ease bodily pain. Since the Sr/Ca ratio follows the main source of calcium in the diet, a regular ash drink would push it up, and the team calculated that even one gram of plant ash a day would be enough.1 There is a modern parallel: bivilviki, a traditional Hopi food of corn mixed with saltbush ash, shapes the bone chemistry of those who eat it even as a minor part of the diet.

Good science asks what else could cause the signal. Minerals in soil can seep into buried bone, so the team tested soils from each burial site, which released strontium and calcium in much the same way, as well as cremated bones that had lain in sealed jars and the woman buried among the gladiators. Those bones had ordinary values, which argues against contamination. A rival explanation is physiological: hard training speeds bone turnover, as studies of triathletes and rugby players show, and that could speed strontium uptake. So the paper says only that the result might suggest an ash drink. It is a strong clue, not a proof.

concepts.title: York's Headless Men and the Lion's Bite
concepts.contentHtml:
Another possible gladiator cemetery lies in northern England. At Driffield Terrace, about a kilometre south-west of the centre of York (Roman Eboracum), excavations in 2004 and 2005 uncovered burials from the first or early second century to the late fourth. It was odd in every way. About 70 per cent of the skeletons well enough preserved to tell had been decapitated, against a usual 5 to 6 per cent in Roman Britain, and most heads had been cut off from behind, a method more often linked with execution.1 Apart from one woman and seven non-adults, everyone was male, aged 18 to 45. Healed injuries were even more common than at Ephesus, 23 per cent against 16, and isotopes and DNA show men from across the empire, one with close genetic links to the Middle East.

In 2025 Tim Thompson of Maynooth University and colleagues re-examined one skeleton, 6DT19, a man aged 26 to 35 who died in the third century. He had been decapitated from behind, and his pelvis bore small puncture marks. The team scanned them in 3D and compared them with bite marks left by cheetahs, lions, tigers and leopards on carcasses at English zoos. Weapon wounds and later damage to the bone did not fit. Their conclusion: a large cat, such as a lion, bit him around the time of death. They called it the first physical evidence for human-animal gladiatorial combat from the Roman period anywhere in Europe.2

Caution is still needed. Some scholars doubt that Driffield Terrace held gladiators at all, preferring captives, criminals or soldiers, and the authors cannot say whether 6DT19 died in a show or an execution.

title: Myth Versus Evidence
description: The thumbs, 'we who are about to die', the real Spartacus, and the women who fought

concepts.title: Which Way Did the Thumb Turn?
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask anyone how a Roman crowd condemned a gladiator and they will turn a thumb down. The ancient texts are far less clear.1 Juvenal writes of fighters who kill "whomsoever the mob with a turn of the thumb bids them slay", and his phrase is pollice verso, "with a turned thumb". It says nothing about up or down.

Other writers muddy the water. Quintilian mentions a hostile thumb, infesto pollice, and a poem collected in the early sixth century links that hostile thumb with a gladiator's death. Yet Pliny the Elder quotes a proverb that bids us turn down our thumbs to show approval. The classicist Anthony Corbeill, in the most thorough study, concludes that a thumb pressed down on the closed fist signalled mercy, while an extended, upright thumb signalled death. If he is right, the modern code is close to backwards. Crowds had other ways to plead, too: Martial says spectators waved handkerchiefs, and they shouted Mitte! ("Let him go!") or Iugula! ("Kill him!"). The final decision belonged to the emperor or, in his absence, the producer of the games.

So where did thumbs down come from? Largely from a painting. Jean-Léon Gérôme began Pollice Verso before 1869, paused during the Franco-Prussian War and finished it in 1872. A victor stands with his foot on the throat of a fallen man, who raises two fingers for mercy, while Vestal Virgins and the crowd turn their thumbs down. Known in English as "Thumbs Down", it fixed the gesture in the modern imagination and inspired Ridley Scott's Gladiator (2000). Phoenix Art Museum, which bought the painting in 1968, says plainly that no historical records confirm the gesture.2

concepts.title: Famous Words and a Famous Rebel
concepts.contentHtml:
"Hail, emperor, those who are about to die salute you." Films put the line in every gladiator's mouth. In the surviving sources it belongs to one famous story. Suetonius describes a sham sea battle that Claudius staged on the Fucine Lake, which he was about to drain. When the combatants cried out the salute, Claudius answered "Or not", one of his feeble jokes. The fighters chose to understand it as a pardon and refused to fight, until the emperor, after hesitating over whether to destroy them all, bullied them into it.1 The speakers were men about to die in a mock naval battle, and it seems not to have been a regular gladiators' greeting at all.

Spartacus has been reshaped even more. The ancient accounts, by Plutarch, Appian and Florus, are dramatic enough. In 73 BCE this Thracian and 78 others broke out of the school of Lentulus Batiatus at Capua, armed with knives and spits from the kitchen. For about two years he beat Roman army after Roman army and gathered, by one account, over 120,000 followers. When his lieutenant Crixus was killed, Spartacus honoured him in the old way, making Roman prisoners fight as gladiators at the funeral. Crassus finally crushed the revolt, and 6,000 survivors were crucified along the Appian Way.

What the sources do not show is a crusade against slavery.2 Plutarch says the original plan was simply to escape, and Spartacus tried to lead his followers out of Italy rather than to change Roman society. The freedom-fighter hero was built much later: by Bernard-Joseph Saurin's French play of 1760, Howard Fast's 1951 novel and Stanley Kubrick's 1960 film, whose "I am Spartacus!" scene came from the blacklisted screenwriter Dalton Trumbo.

concepts.title: Women in the Arena
concepts.contentHtml:
Did women fight as gladiators? Yes, though rarely, and the best evidence is a slab of marble. A relief from Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum, Turkey), carved in the first or second century CE and now in the British Museum, shows two women fighters on a platform with spectators' heads on either side. Each is named, with stage names borrowed from myth: Amazon, after the warrior women, and Achilia, after the hero Achilles.

Above them is carved the Greek word APELUTHESAN, "they were freed". The relief commemorates their honourable release from service, which they won after a series of outstanding performances.1 These two women did not die in the arena; they earned their way out of it.

Written sources confirm that women entered the arena. At the opening of the Colosseum in 80 CE, Cassius Dio says, women helped kill the animals, though "not those of any prominence". Tacitus was scandalised that in 63 CE, under Nero, distinguished women as well as senators appeared in the arena in record numbers.

Then came the ban, and its trigger is a surprise. Women were permitted to fight until Septimius Severus outlawed it in 200 CE.2 Dio, who lived through it, explains why: at a gymnastic contest women competed so fiercely that jokes were made about other very distinguished women, and "therefore it was henceforth forbidden for any woman, no matter what her origin, to fight in single combat". The spark was athletics and gossip about the elite, not a gladiator fight. How strictly the ban was enforced afterwards is unknown.

title: Beasts, Chariots and the End of the Games
description: Beast hunts and the animal trade, the Circus Maximus and its stars, the Nika riot, and the last shows

concepts.title: Venationes: An Empire Brought to the Arena
concepts.contentHtml:
Before the gladiators came the animals. Morning programmes featured venationes, staged hunts in which trained hunters, the venatores, faced lions, tigers and leopards, bears, elephants, wild boar, stags and bulls, often in an arena landscaped with rocks and trees to look like some distant land. Animals were also agents of execution. Criminals, war captives and others, Christians among them, were condemned to the beasts.

The numbers are staggering. Augustus boasted that 3,500 animals were killed in the 26 hunts of his reign. The opening of the Colosseum killed somewhere between five and ten thousand, depending on the source, and Trajan's celebration of his conquest of Dacia some eleven thousand. Pompey showed elephants, and Rome's first rhinoceros, in the Circus Maximus, partly to prove his power over even the strongest beasts. One account goes further, claiming that capture for the games drove hippopotamuses out of Nubia and elephants out of northern Africa. That is hard to separate from other pressures and is best treated as uncertain.

Every animal had to be caught, caged and shipped alive, and the York lion shows how far that network reached. The 2025 study argues that moving ferae africanae, the Roman term for the lions and leopards of the arena, as far as Britain implies boxes and cages, ships and wagons, keepers and trainers, and food on the hoof. Corporations of animal hunters like the Telegenii, known from Tunisia, may have supplied the experts.1 A late third-century mosaic at Rudston in Yorkshire even names its animal stars: a lion called Leo Flammefer, "the fiery lion", and a bull called Taurus Omicida, "Killer the bull".

concepts.title: The Circus Maximus and the Richest Athlete in History
concepts.contentHtml:
Gladiators drew crowds, but the chariot races drew far more. The Circus Maximus, in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills, was Rome's oldest and largest public space. After its rebuilding following the fire of 64 CE it held some 250,000 spectators, five times the Colosseum. The sand track measured about 540 by 80 metres. Chariots burst from 12 starting gates and raced seven laps around a central barrier decorated with obelisks, with each lap counted off by markers shaped like eggs and dolphins.

Drivers came from the lower orders of society but raced for colour-coded teams, the factions: Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues. The factions were businesses that invested heavily in horses and equipment, and their fans were fanatical. Some arrived the evening before to stake out good seats, and fans hurled lead curse amulets, punctured with nails, at rival teams.

The greatest earner was Gaius Appuleius Diocles, a Lusitanian Spaniard who had short stints with the Whites and Greens before a long career with the Reds. Over 24 years he won 35,863,120 sesterces in prize money.1 The total is recorded on a monument that his fellow charioteers and admirers set up in Rome in 146 CE, when he retired at the age of "42 years, 7 months, and 23 days". The classicist Peter Struck calculates that it was five times the earnings of the best-paid provincial governors over a similar period: enough to supply grain to the whole city of Rome for a year, or to pay the Roman army's ordinary soldiers for a fifth of a year. Scale that army pay to the wages of the American armed forces and Diocles made about $15 billion.

concepts.title: Nika! and the Last Shows
concepts.contentHtml:
The factions outlived the western empire. In Constantinople's Hippodrome the Blues and Greens dominated the fifth and sixth centuries and were notorious for violence. In January 532 Justinian refused to pardon Blue and Green supporters after a recent riot, and the rivals joined forces under their racing chant, Nika! ("Conquer!"). They burned Hagia Sophia and the Senate House and crowned a rival emperor, Hypatios. Justinian's generals Belisarius and Mundus then slaughtered 30,000 people inside the Hippodrome.1 Were the factions political parties? Older reference works tied the Greens to the lower classes and Monophysite Christianity and the Blues to orthodoxy and the upper classes. More recent accounts see no fixed political or social programme, just fan groups that could be drawn into politics.

Gladiators had gone long before. Constantine issued the first ban in 325, yet earlier in his reign he had sent a multitude of conquered barbarians to their deaths in the amphitheatre at Trier, and the edict had no lasting effect except at Constantinople, which never saw gladiators fight. Honorius closed the remaining schools in 399. The bishop Theodoret tells how a monk named Telemachus stepped down into the arena at Rome to separate two fighters and was stoned to death by the angry crowd, after which Honorius ended the shows, traditionally in 404. Yet no law of Honorius on the subject survives, so the story may compress a slower decline.2

The animals lasted longest. Beast hunts went on until they were abolished in 523, and the last chariot race in the Circus Maximus was held in 549 by Totila, king of the Ostrogoths. Nearly eight centuries after three pairs fought in a cattle market, Rome's games ended not with one decree but with a long fade.
